title: 2 Samuel 22:17–31
context: The LORD draws David out of danger, and David speaks of his covenant integrity and of God’s just dealings with the merciful, the pure, the afflicted, and the arrogant, ending in praise of God’s perfect way and tested word.

verses.text: He sent from on high and he took me. He drew me out of many waters.
verses.arminianNotes: “He sent from on high and he took me. He drew me out of many waters.” Arminian readers see God personally rescuing his servant from overwhelming danger.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see deliverance as God’s initiative. The image of being drawn out of waters returns to the floods of verse 5, now overcome.

verses.text: He delivered me from my strong enemy, from those who hated me, for they were too mighty for me.
verses.arminianNotes: “He delivered me from my strong enemy, from those who hated me, for they were too mighty for me.” Arminian readers see honest acknowledgment of human weakness and divine help.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see dependence on God confessed. David admits the enemy was too strong for him, making the rescue entirely God’s work.

verses.text: They came on me in the day of my calamity, but the LORD was my support.
verses.arminianNotes: “They came on me in the day of my calamity, but the LORD was my support.” Arminian readers see God standing with his servant in the hardest moment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God upholding David in calamity. The verse is shared ground for readers in both traditions: the LORD supports those who trust him.

verses.text: He also brought me out into a large place. He delivered me, because he delighted in me.
verses.arminianNotes: “He delivered me, because he delighted in me.” Arminian readers see God’s pleasure in a servant who walked faithfully with him and relied on him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s delight as the ground of deliverance. Many in this tradition see that delight rooted in God’s gracious choice of David before any merit.

verses.text: The LORD rewarded me according to my righteousness. He rewarded me according to the cleanness of my hands.
verses.arminianNotes: “The LORD rewarded me according to my righteousness.” Arminian readers read this in literary context as covenant loyalty and integrity, especially in David’s conduct toward Saul, not a claim of sinless perfection.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read it as covenant faithfulness rather than self-earned standing. Many in this tradition also stress that such integrity is itself the fruit of God’s grace at work in David.

verses.text: For I have kept the LORD’s ways, and have not wickedly departed from my God.
verses.arminianNotes: “For I have kept the LORD’s ways, and have not wickedly departed from my God.” Arminian readers see sincere faithfulness that God honors, without denying David’s later sins.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a claim of covenant loyalty, not flawlessness. Readers in this tradition often note that the song is set in the context of David’s deliverance from Saul.

verses.text: For all his ordinances were before me. As for his statutes, I didn’t depart from them.
verses.arminianNotes: “For all his ordinances were before me. As for his statutes, I didn’t depart from them.” Arminian readers see God’s law guiding a life of faithful obedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see devotion to God’s word as a mark of true faith. The verse expresses the orientation of David’s life rather than claiming he never failed.

verses.text: I was also perfect toward him. I kept myself from my iniquity.
verses.arminianNotes: “I was also perfect toward him. I kept myself from my iniquity.” Arminian readers see “perfect” as wholeheartedness and integrity, in keeping with the song’s context.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read “perfect” as blamelessness in covenant relationship. Readers in this tradition generally hold that this language does not contradict the confession of sin found elsewhere in David’s story.

verses.text: Therefore the LORD has rewarded me according to my righteousness, According to my cleanness in his eyesight.
verses.arminianNotes: “Therefore the LORD has rewarded me according to my righteousness.” Arminian readers see God faithfully responding to a life of integrity, which encourages faithfulness in others.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s faithfulness to his covenant servant. Readers in both traditions commonly take these verses as describing integrity within a gracious covenant, not earning God’s favor.

verses.text: With the merciful you will show yourself merciful. With the perfect man you will show yourself perfect.
verses.arminianNotes: “With the merciful you will show yourself merciful. With the perfect man you will show yourself perfect.” Arminian readers see God’s dealings fitting the character of those who respond to him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s consistency in dealing with people. The verse describes how God’s faithfulness meets the faithful, a principle readers apply with care.

verses.text: With the pure you will show yourself pure. With the crooked you will show yourself shrewd.
verses.arminianNotes: “With the pure you will show yourself pure. With the crooked you will show yourself shrewd.” Arminian readers see God responding justly to each person’s chosen path.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s justice adapting to human crookedness. The verse warns that no one can outmaneuver God by deceit or cunning.

verses.text: You will save the afflicted people, but your eyes are on the arrogant, that you may bring them down.
verses.arminianNotes: “You will save the afflicted people, but your eyes are on the arrogant, that you may bring them down.” Arminian readers see God’s compassion for the humble and opposition to pride.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God exalting the lowly and humbling the proud. The theme echoes Hannah’s song in 1 Samuel 2, framing the books of Samuel.

verses.text: For you are my lamp, LORD. The LORD will light up my darkness.
verses.arminianNotes: “For you are my lamp, LORD. The LORD will light up my darkness.” Arminian readers see God as the believer’s guide through danger and uncertainty.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God as the source of light and life. The image recalls “the lamp of Israel” in 21:17, now applied to the LORD himself.

verses.text: For by you, I run against a troop. By my God, I leap over a wall.
verses.arminianNotes: “For by you, I run against a troop. By my God, I leap over a wall.” Arminian readers see God empowering his servant for tasks beyond human strength.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see all strength coming from God. The verse credits David’s military achievements to God’s enabling power.

verses.text: As for God, his way is perfect. The LORD’s word is tested. He is a shield to all those who take refuge in him.
verses.arminianNotes: “As for God, his way is perfect. The LORD’s word is tested.” Arminian readers see God’s reliability as the foundation for trusting him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s word proved true. The closing line, “He is a shield to all those who take refuge in him,” is shared ground on God’s faithfulness.
